verses.text: “You shall make the altar of acacia wood, five cubits  long, and five cubits wide; the altar shall be square: and its height shall be three cubits.
You shall make its horns on its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it; and you shall overlay it with brass.
You shall make its pots to take away its ashes, its shovels, its basins, its meat hooks, and its fire pans: all its vessels you shall make of brass.
You shall make a grating for it of network of brass: and on the net you shall make four bronze rings in its four corners.
You shall put it under the ledge around the altar beneath, that the net may reach halfway up the altar.
You shall make poles for the altar, poles of acacia wood, and overlay them with brass.
Its poles shall be put into the rings, and the poles shall be on the two sides of the altar, when carrying it.
You shall make it with hollow planks. They shall make it as it has been shown you on the mountain.
“You shall make the court of the tabernacle: for the south side southward there shall be hangings for the court of fine twined linen one hundred cubits long for one side:
and its pillars shall be twenty, and their sockets twenty, of brass; the hooks of the pillars and their fillets shall be of silver.

Likewise for the north side in length there shall be hangings one hundred cubits long, and its pillars twenty, and their sockets twenty, of brass; the hooks of the pillars, and their fillets, of silver.
For the width of the court on the west side shall be hangings of fifty cubits; their pillars ten, and their sockets ten.
The width of the court on the east side eastward shall be fifty cubits.
The hangings for the one side of the gate shall be fifteen cubits; their pillars three, and their sockets three.
For the other side shall be hangings of fifteen cubits; their pillars three, and their sockets three.
For the gate of the court shall be a screen of twenty cubits, of blue, and purple, and scarlet, and fine twined linen, the work of the embroiderer; their pillars four, and their sockets four.
All the pillars of the court around shall be filleted with silver; their hooks of silver, and their sockets of brass.
The length of the court shall be one hundred cubits, and the width fifty every where, and the height five cubits, of fine twined linen, and their sockets of brass.
All the instruments of the tabernacle in all its service, and all its pins, and all the pins of the court, shall be of brass.
“You shall command the children of Israel, that they bring to you pure olive oil beaten for the light, to cause a lamp to burn continually.

In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil which is before the testimony, Aaron and his sons shall keep it in order from evening to morning before Yahweh: it shall be a statute forever throughout their generations on the behalf of the children of Israel.

footnotes.content: The altar of acacia wood, square and three cubits high—a humble platform for the most important work in Israel. Here the costly offering goes up, and the Lord draws near to receive what belongs to Him. The wood is acacia, the same tree that frames the wilderness path; nothing grand, but built to stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The horns of the altar, one piece with the whole—a place of refuge where the guilty could grip them and find mercy. Even the design of the altar speaks of sanctuary, reminding us that sin met here is not met with abandonment, but with a way home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ash shovels, meat hooks, fire pans—the whole service requires vessels for the work. But I notice: each tool is made of the same brass, the same humble material. The Lord does not require finery for the tools of worship, only faithful hands and faithful hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A brass grating of network, with rings at the four corners—a cage to hold the burning wood and the offering safe. The fire will not consume what is not meant to be consumed. There is order in this place, even in the flames.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The grating reaches halfway up—a measured mercy. It contains the hottest part of the offering but does not hide it from the priest's sight. All the work is visible to those who serve; there is no cover for negligence in the Lord's house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Acacia poles overlaid with brass—even the means of carrying the altar must be beautiful and strong. When the sanctuary moves, what bears the altar of offering moves with sacred dignity.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The poles on two sides, the rings receiving them—a pattern of partnership. No single person carries the altar alone; it takes community and strength from both sides to bear the place where sins are answered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Made of hollow planks, built according to what was shown on the mountain—the pattern comes from above, not from human invention. We do not design worship; we remember the pattern the Lord has given and follow it faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hundred cubits of fine linen for the south side—the courtyard is made beautiful and holy, woven with care and ordered grace. The place where God meets His people is not a rushing, common space but marked apart, dignified, prepared for encounter.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Twenty pillars of brass with silver hooks—the pillars hold the linen up, and silver catches the light. Even what supports the boundary of holy ground is made with beauty. The Lord's orderliness shows us that care in the smallest things honors Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The north side mirrors the south—the courtyard is even, balanced, speaking of fairness and justice. As the Lord's mercy is ordered and sure, so too is His judgment; both come to all alike.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The west side is fifty cubits, shorter than the north and south—not every side needs the same measure; each has its place and purpose. Faithfulness means knowing where to be smaller and where to be larger.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The east side, where the morning comes first—facing the rising light, open to the coming day. The courtyard receives God's mercies that are new each morning, and the place is oriented to meet them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One side of the gate, fifteen cubits—the entrance to holy ground requires passage, a threshold, a turning point. Not every soul walks carelessly into the Lord's presence; you must come through the gate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The other side of the gate, also fifteen cubits—the Lord's welcome is both sides of the doorway. We come in, and we go out; both movements are held within the grace that guards this place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A screen of blue, purple, and scarlet—woven by embroiderers' hands, colors that speak of heaven, royalty, and blood. The gate into the courtyard is beautiful and costly; it is not a casual passage but a costly crossing to meet the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Silver filleting around the whole court—the metal of redemption adorns every support, every hook, every connection. The whole structure is marked with the token of price paid, ransomed beauty.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hundred cubits long, fifty wide, five cubits high—the courtyard has measure and boundary. It is not boundless or shapeless; it is defined, knowable, a space where the Lord's people can stand without wandering lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All instruments brass, all pins brass—not one pin of lesser metal in the Lord's house. From the greatest vessel to the smallest fastening, everything that holds the sanctuary together is fashioned with the same careful material. Unity in the work.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pure olive oil beaten for the light—oil pressed by labor to burn continually, a light that will not go out. The Lord asks Israel to bring forth what is costly and true, so that the lamp may burn without ceasing before His face.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Aaron and his sons keep the lamp in order, evening to morning, a statute forever—and readers today hear an echo of this faithfulness. Someone must tend the light, generation after generation; the work of keeping watch never ends, but the covenant promises it will be remembered.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
